summary: A satirical account of a city's public works budget process in fall 2023, following department pitches from water, roads and urban planning, then financial analysts, compliance, public input, consultants and a failed budget trick. The piece mocks bureaucratic loops, cost overruns and civic theater, concluding that the cycle of funding debates continues with no resolution.
one_line: A satirical chronicle of a city's 2023 public works budget season, from department pitches to consultants, overruns and endless indecision.
key_facts: The budget saga begins after September 1st, 2023, as city officials allocate the annual public works budget.
On September 15th, Mayor Linda Evergreen presides over the first meeting on the upcoming fiscal year's finances.
Barry Cistern heads the Department of Pipe Dreams and Waterworks and requests $50 million to replace the city's aging water pipes.
On September 23rd, Frank Tarley of the Department of Ground Control pitches a roughly $50 million request to fix potholes, using a PowerPoint deck with clip art.
Penelope Perspective leads the Visionaries of Urban Planning, whose monorail plan carries a $200 million price tag that sparks chaos on the floor.
On October 3rd, financial analysts point out that the city's treasury resembles a piggy bank after an encounter with a hammer.
On October 10th, compliance expert Sir Reginald Redtape explains that every million spent brings a tall stack of paperwork.
Autumn town hall meetings for public input are portrayed as sound bites and lip service, a recurring sketch of municipal theater.
In November external consultants arrive, charging fees that never seem to be below six figures, and offer a blueprint resembling last year's with new jargon.
On December 2nd, Ima Moneykeeper of the Budgetary Illusions Department makes projected deficits vanish into surpluses, until a junior analyst debunks the act.
December ends with groundbreaking ceremonies, and construction delays and cost overruns are compared to the myth of Sisyphus.
The article ends without a conclusion, noting the cycle continues and that local governance remains a spectacle for those with a taste for civic satire.
